analysis.one_liner: Delays Medicare price negotiation for pill-based drugs from 7 to 11 years after approval.
analysis.headline: Introduced March 4, 2025 with 7 Republican cosponsors; referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has seen no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare now negotiates prices for its most expensive drugs, but only after a drug has been on the market for at least 7 years for pill-based (small-molecule) drugs or 11 years for biologic drugs. This bill would require pill-based drugs to also sit on the market for at least 11 years before they can be negotiated, starting in 2028. That four-year delay means brand-name pill makers keep their prices higher for longer before Medicare can negotiate them down.
analysis.who_benefits: Brand-name drug companies that sell pill-based (small-molecule) medicines, especially makers of high-spending Medicare drugs, gain roughly four more years of un-negotiated list prices on each qualifying drug. The bill's supporters also argue the change removes a bias against pills and preserves investment in new pill-based medicines.

how_it_helps.text: The bill raises the market-approval requirement for a pill-based drug to qualify for Medicare price negotiation from 7 years to 11 years, beginning with the 2028 negotiation cycle.
The stated purpose is to equalize the negotiation period between small-molecule drugs and biologics, since biologics already face an 11-year wait before negotiation.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers, who would keep paying un-negotiated brand-name prices for pill drugs for up to four extra years before those prices can be negotiated down.

drawbacks.text: Delaying negotiation eligibility by four years postpones the price savings Medicare's negotiation program was designed to produce, raising drug spending for beneficiaries and the federal government during those years.
The bill contains no offsetting provision to lower drug prices or protect patients; its sole effect is to postpone when Medicare can negotiate.

Supporters' good-faith objection: because biologics already get an 11-year window, the current 7-year window for pills treats pill-based medicines less favorably and, they argue, could discourage development of new pills, which are often cheaper and easier for patients to take than injected biologics. The counterpoint is that pills are also typically cheaper to develop and manufacture, so equalizing the wait shifts billions in costs to Medicare rather than to R&D risk.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The genuine policy question—whether the 7-year pill window discourages new pill development—is real but narrow. The bill answers it in the most one-sided way possible: by delaying price negotiation on some of Medicare's highest-spending pills for four years, with no savings, caps, or patient protections added anywhere else in the bill. The cost lands on seniors and taxpayers; the benefit lands on the drugmakers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was filed, and the committee has not taken it up since.

narrative.text: Sen. Tillis introduced the bill on March 4, 2025, joined by Sens. Budd, Blackburn, Daines, and Lankford on introduction.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day, and no markup, hearing, or vote has followed.
Seven Republican senators are listed as cosponsors, with no Democratic cosponsors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost—the bill has not moved, and Medicare's current negotiation timeline stays in place until Congress changes it.

for.name: Sen. Thom Tillis
for.role: U.S. Senator from North Carolina; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the EPIC Act and recruited cosponsors

for.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
for.role: Industry backers of delaying the Medicare negotiation timeline for small-molecule drugs
for.what_they_did: Publicly pressed Congress to extend the small-molecule negotiation window, framing it as fixing the IRA's so-called pill penalty

sides.party_line_note: All sponsors and all 7 cosponsors are Republicans; no Democrat has signed on, and no member of either party has taken action against it because the bill has not moved beyond referral.

industries.note: Each qualifying pill drug would stay off Medicare's negotiation list for four extra years, preserving monopoly list prices on some of the program's highest-spending medicines. The industry's gain comes directly out of the savings seniors and taxpayers would otherwise get from negotiation.

The bill leaves the biologics negotiation window at 11 years, so it neither helps nor hurts them directly. Its indirect effect is to keep cheaper pill alternatives' prices high longer, which can reduce competitive pressure on biologic prices too.

Delaying when Medicare negotiates a drug also delays the market dynamics that push toward lower-cost generic competition, so generic makers gain nothing from this bill and their products stay less affordable relative to brand prices for longer.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Senate Finance Committee with 7 of 53 Republican cosponsors and no Democratic support. As a standalone bill it is unlikely to get floor time this Congress; the realistic path is that its language gets folded into a larger tax or health package, where the pharmaceutical industry's 'pill penalty fix' has drawn bipartisan interest, or it simply expires at the end of the 119th Congress like most referred bills.
